doc.title: Danny Barker Interview (Louis Armstrong memorial broadcast), 1971-07-09

title: Fred Robbins recalls his last visit with Armstrong
summary: After What a Wonderful World, Fred Robbins describes visiting Armstrong at home on his 71st birthday and his humility, humor and love.

story.theme_name: Illness, injury and the deaths of colleagues
story.community_name: Illness, injury and death among jazz musicians

blocks.x: I see trees of green, red and blue and stew. I see them bloom, from me and you. And I think to myself, what a wonderful world. What a wonderful world. I see skies of blue and clouds of white. The bright, blessed day. The bright, blessed day. The dark, sacred night. And I think to myself, what a wonderful world. What a wonderful world. The colors of the rainbow. So pretty in the sky. Are also on the faces of people going by. I see friends shaking in. Saying, how do you do? They're really saying, I love you. I hear pages cry. I watch them grow. They're not much more. And I'll never know. I see friends shaking in. Saying, how do you do? They're really saying, I love you. I hear pages cry. I watch them grow. They're not much more. Then I'll never know. And I think to myself.

Now, Louis Armstrong's wonderful world is just a little of Louis' Fred Robbins. I'm so glad I went to see Louis Armstrong on Sunday, his birthday, 71st, at his home in Corona. I never would have forgiven myself if I hadn't. I was on the way back from the beach and we called, of course, in advance to find out if he was okay. And his wonderful wife, Lucille, said, sure, drop in. I'd been at his home several times before on his birthday. But this was the most important. He looked fine. His face was fuller. He was having his chicken dinner, watching television. We spent about an hour with him. And he was in wonderful spirits. He talked about going back to work in the fall in Las Vegas. And that he'd been warming up on his horn every day. He felt better. His appetite was fine. And then he went through quite a siege in the hospital. Didn't really know how sick he was. Had all the nurses in stitches, telling him stories as he always did. Later, of course, they told him how seriously ill he was. He said, I guess it just wasn't my time, Pops. And then the next day it was his time. He was such a remarkable man. Really a big kid. And a very simple man. And a man that just exuded love for everybody, all kinds of people. And people loved him in return. If you mentioned Louie's name anywhere, it would provoke a smile. That was the image. Fun and jollity and goodness. I guess he was probably the greatest goodwill ambassador our country has ever had. There's no question of that. He did more for the good name and the good feeling toward America than anybody. And in every corner of the world. And if you stop and think, he is or was the most famous American in the world. Better known than anybody. Any scientist, any sports figure, any motion picture star. The best known American any place in the world. Everyone knew Louie Armstrong. The amazing thing about Pops is that with all that success and fame and adulation and adoration and the fact that he played for kings and had audiences with popes and had been everywhere, he was really a simple, unpretentious man. He had a modest home in Corona, Queens where he's lived for 30 years. A marvelous wife, Lucille, whom he met at the Cotton Club. Gave him 30 years of great, great happiness. And I guess it was just innate in his character to have this wonderful humility about him, despite his greatness. The stories, the mother wit that he had, the earthy humor, was also very much a part of Pops. He was one of the greatest storytellers ever. You could mention any subject. Anybody's name, he'd have a story about it. And he'd have you rolling on the floor. And what jokes, you know. Really a happy man all through his life. But in a world that has so much turmoil, the most important thing to Louis was love. He knew that that was what the world needs then and now. Love. And he spread a lot of joy to the world through his great artistry, his playing, his singing, his incomparable performances everywhere. He spread a lot of sunshine around. He made the world a better place for having been in it. He was loved. And, of course, he'll be missed terribly. Because everything came from him. He was the source. The best popular artists today is a little bit of Louis in all of them. Anybody who plays jazz anywhere, I mean, Pops laid it down.
